## Resume essentials

Note: I did not search the web for this answer (web search was unavailable), so anything about Northwind Analytics beyond the posting text itself is marked [unverified]. Figures and quotes taken directly from the posting are not marked, since the posting is the source in front of me; I have not independently verified Northwind Analytics as a real, operating company.

The posting's own language to mirror on your resume: "customer interviews," "requirements," "backlog," "prioritised," "product metrics (adoption, retention, time-to-plan)," "experiments," "release coordination," "SQL," "Jira," "agile," "scrum."

- **Customer-facing problem-finding** ("Interview customers and analyse support tickets to find the problems worth solving"). Your background already shows direct customer contact: "Summer 2026 intern at a family-owned moving company in Phoenix: answered customer calls and logged complaints in a shared spreadsheet." Frame this explicitly as customer-issue triage — e.g., "Logged and categorized customer complaint calls, surfacing recurring issues for [owner/manager]." Use a placeholder like [X number] of calls or [X%] recurring-issue rate only if you can fill in a real figure — do not invent one.
- **Leading a project/team.** Your background shows this directly: "Events chair of the PM Club for two semesters: ran 5 events and grew average attendance from 22 to 41 students." This maps cleanly to the posting's "Evidence of leading a project or team." State it close to verbatim since these are your own reported numbers: "Grew average event attendance from 22 to 41 students (+86%) across 5 events as Events Chair, PM Club."
- **Comfort with data / spreadsheets.** Your background shows: "Built a Google Sheets tracker for club sign-ups." Call this out explicitly as a spreadsheet-tools bullet, since "spreadsheets required" is stated verbatim in the posting: "Built and maintained a Google Sheets tracker for club event sign-ups."
- **Written communication.** Not directly evidenced in what you've told me. Where it does not show yet: a cover letter, a short writing sample, or a line noting you wrote recaps/communications for the PM Club would be the kind of evidence to add — e.g., "Wrote weekly event recap emails to [X] club members" (fill in a real number, don't invent one).
- **SQL.** Your gap list says "No SQL." The posting marks SQL as "a plus," not required, so do not claim it. Where it does not show: a completed short SQL course or a small personal project with a real platform name and completion date would be the kind of evidence to add before application day if time allows.
- **Curiosity about logistics and supply chains.** Not directly evidenced yet. Where it does not show: a line connecting your moving-company internship to logistics interest would help, e.g., "Developed interest in operations and logistics while handling customer complaint calls at [company], noticing patterns in scheduling delays" — only use specifics you can actually verify of your own experience.

## Handling your gaps

**Gap 1: No SQL.**
Honest, confident framing: say plainly that you haven't used SQL yet, but that you're comfortable with structured data (your Google Sheets tracker is real evidence) and you pick up technical tools quickly. Avoid claiming SQL skill you don't have — interviewers in PM roles often probe with a quick follow-up question.
Concrete step before the interview: complete a short, free introductory SQL tutorial (for example, a well-known platform's beginner SQL module — note: I have not verified a specific course name or provider, so treat any such name as [unverified] until you confirm it yourself) and be ready to say which one and what you covered.

**Gap 2: Never worked in software.**
Honest, confident framing: acknowledge it directly, then redirect to the transferable parts of your experience — handling real customer complaints in a structured way (the moving-company log) and running a project with measurable outcomes (the PM Club events). Make the case that the core APM skills (talking to customers, organizing information, driving a project to a result) transfer across industries, and that "new graduates welcome" signals the company expects to train the software-specific parts.
Concrete step before the interview: read two or three of Northwind Analytics' own product pages or blog posts (if available) and prepare one specific observation about their route-planning product, so you can speak knowledgeably about the domain even without prior software experience. Note: I could not verify what, if anything, Northwind Analytics publishes online, since this is a fictional/test posting and I did not search the web.

## Questions to prepare for

- "Walk me through a time you led a project or team." — Shows whether you can structure a STAR-style answer and whether your PM Club leadership story demonstrates real ownership and measurable impact.
- "Tell me about a time you had to deal with a frustrated or unhappy customer." — Shows how you handle the "talk to customers every week" core of the role; your moving-company call-logging experience is directly relevant here.
- "How do you prioritize when you have more to do than time allows?" — Shows whether you can reason about tradeoffs the way the "keep the backlog prioritised" responsibility requires.
- "What would you do if engineering told you a requested feature would take twice as long as expected?" — Shows how you'd handle the engineer/designer coordination side of the job under pressure.
- "You don't have a software or SQL background — how do you plan to get up to speed?" — Shows self-awareness and a concrete plan rather than defensiveness; this is the direct question behind your stated gaps.
- "Why Northwind Analytics, and why this role specifically?" — Shows whether you've actually read the posting and thought about the logistics/route-planning domain versus generic PM interest.
- "Tell me about a metric you tracked over time and what you learned from it." — Shows whether you can connect to "Track product metrics ... and report on them monthly"; your club attendance numbers (22 to 41) are a usable example if framed as a tracked metric.

## Smart questions to ask

1. "The posting mentions shipping improvements every two weeks — what does that two-week cycle actually look like day to day for an associate PM?"
2. "How does the team decide which customer-reported problems from support tickets get prioritized over others on the roadmap?"
3. "What does success look like for someone in this role at the 6-month mark versus the 1-year mark?"
4. "How involved is the associate PM in the monthly metrics reporting — is that more data-pulling, or more presenting and interpreting?"
5. "The company has grown 40% a year for three years — how has that growth changed how the product team works, and is that pace expected to continue?"
6. "Since this product is specifically route-planning for logistics companies, what's a customer problem the team is currently trying to solve that I might be able to help think through?"

Note: Question 5 restates a figure from the posting itself ("grown 40% a year for three years"), not a verified external fact — treat it as [unverified] beyond what the posting states.

## Summary

For the Northwind Analytics Associate PM role, lead your resume with the PM Club leadership numbers (22→41 attendance, 5 events) and the Google Sheets tracker as direct evidence of leadership and spreadsheet comfort, and frame the moving-company internship as customer-problem-finding experience. Address the two stated gaps — no SQL and no software-industry experience — with a short pre-interview SQL tutorial and a plan to connect transferable customer/leadership skills to the role, since the posting explicitly welcomes new graduates.
